projectDesc.p: The Middle English Texts Series offers a diverse and representative array of literary texts that medieval readers in the present-day British Isles would have encountered between the twelfth and sixteenth centuries. It is committed to making available both affordable print and open access editions to scholars, teachers, and students of the Western Middle Ages. In its digital publications, the series prioritizes a user-friendly interface and viewing options, multiple downloadable formats, enhanced searchability and filtering, and accessibility to the widest possible range of users.

editorialDecl.p: METS takes as its mission the creation of affordable editions that would pass scrutiny from the most demanding expert, yet would prove comprehensible, and even enticing, to someone who had never read Middle English before. This agenda dictates that METS publications offer not a critical edition reflecting all surviving manuscripts, and certainly not a diplomatic edition, but a best-text edition, informed by the notes and apparatus of earlier editions (where these exist), and by substantive variants from other manuscript witnesses. Transcriptions of Middle English texts are lightly modernized to ensure a smooth reading experience, while non-English texts preserve both the original language and a modern English translation in facing-page format. Each edition offers expert assistance with language and lexicon, providing glosses alongside the text(s), textual and explanatory notes, elucidation of unfamiliar contexts and traditions, and thematic and interpretive possibilities. All editions feature general introductions that set the edited text within its own time, place, and traditions, and link it to ancestor, congener, and successor materials. All publications contain comprehensive, current bibliographies of pertinent scholarship and criticism. House style is adapted from the Chicago Manual of Style.

ab.foreign: Tria sunt opera sapientis: facere de inimico amicum, de nesciente scientem, de malo bonum. Hec

And of il disposed in wykkednesse,

ab.foreign: Nullus debet dominari nisi pius. Decet reges non dare posse nec dominium, nisi pietatem habentibus; et ex hoc diliget omnes sicut bonus pater bonos filios. Hec

lg.l: A king aught not to geve auctorité,
Might, power, lordeship, ne also puissance,Gpower
But to piteous men of equité,
For no praier, grete requeste, or instance:

Ye shul love al folkesT in charité,
As the fader the sone, with grete pité.

ab.foreign: Vita hominis est tam brevis quod quis non haberent alium in odio. Hec
Et tractetis amicos
vestros cum amore, vero, nec ostendatis una hora signum odii.

lg.l: Considre that your liff is shorte and brief
In this transitory world,N and passing.
Therfore, for a goode and blessed relieff,
Ye aught not to have other in hatyng,

Neither wronging theim bi extorcion,
Ner plukkingG theim als bi compulsion.urging

ab.foreign: Qui non bene faciat amicis cum potest, deserent eum cum indigebit eisdem. Hec

lg.l: Cherissh wele your freendes while that ye may,
As wele in worde as preferryng,Gas in advancement
Showyng theim semblance of love every day,
CorogengG theim to be to you lovyng.Encouraging
Thus your glorious fame shal be springing
To high and lowe of your noble kyndnesse.
Who is he that wold nat please your highnesse?

ab.foreign: Tria sunt que regibus obsunt: superflua vini potacio, musicorum frequens auditus, et amor nimis mulierum. Hec

lg.l: That kyng that maketh his region

ab.foreign: Quando volueris consulere aliquem super factis tuis, investiga illum, qualiter seipsum gubernet in suis; quia si videris eum non dirigere animam suam, nec studere quod aliquas bonitates adquirat, multo plus tui negligens erit cum te minori precio reputet quam seipsum. Hec

lg.l: Yf ye wol aske counsaile of any man,

ab.foreign: Sis vigilans in tuo consilio, quia dormire in eo est participare cum morte. Hec

lg.l: Why dothe a wytty man aske counsaile?

lg.l: Yf any people holde you vertuous,
Goode, gentil, kinde, curteise with al mekenesse,
To repute hym trewe be right labourous,
Whether he be lowe or in grete highnesse.
He that hathe grete labour and besynesse,
How shold he reule and governe many moo?N

WhatG men wol saien of thereG governance,N That their

servitur, et sunt hii: gratias age si aliquid impenditur tibi; si male habueris, sustine

For to be doon in eny maner wise,

lg.l: By thre thinges is knowen a wiseman:

Not to be elate,G ne in pride therfore,haughty

bonis. Hec

Ye muste kepe in your noble memory

Not in estate, nor clothinges richely,

note.gloss: The present little book, compiled, extracted, and translated into English in a poem by George Ashby, lately clerk of the signet for our supreme lady Margaret, Queen of England, etc., by the grace of God, from the good favor, love, and heartfelt affection which he himself by natural law bears to such a degree towards her high stature and royal majesty, and towards his mightiest and most excellent lord, Edward, by the same grace the firstborn son of our supreme Lord King Henry and of his queen consort, Prince of Wales, Duke of Cornwall, and Earl of Chester, for whose love and pleasure this compilation is made . . . his noble blood, under which he himself has been kept and brought up since his youth up until now, and never in his whole life in another’s service. It is divided into three times: namely, in the past, the present, and the future. The past stimulates to more often remember past things so well, through reading sacred scripture and chronicles as well as other accounts and experiences . . . He himself can perfectly discern the goodness of good deeds and the opinion of books, and the misery and ruin of wrongdoers and of the miserable . . . whence he can govern himself wisely and happily. The present shows how he should bear himself in wisdom and policy, with deeds pleasing to God and his people, and for his own security. The future discreetly and prudently grants foresight into future matters . . . in guiding himself with honor, blessed fame, and good governance, and in avoiding damages, accusations, and discomforts. Furthermore, to be in the future active in policy and wisdom . . . for the security and good custody of his subjects, under debt and faithful obedience, through the advice, dicts, and sayings of diverse philosophers, whose names . . . are briefly recorded in this treatise.

Now of the present time
It is fitting for the king to pay his retainers their wages for military service, or else the community will despise him and his rule. Thus Plato.
The foundation of the fear of God is piety. Thus Pythagoras.
Both on the inside and on the outside, you should be such as you speak: in turn, what you express in your speech should not be different from what you keep in your heart. Thus Hermes.
Now of the future
Let quickly be sufficient whatever is good
You should do unto others what you want to be done to yourself, and not do unto others what you do not want to be done to yourself. Thus Socrates.

You should quickly inflict punishment on wrongdoers of the realm, based on what is known of their offence. And he who hinders your rule, decapitate him publicly, in order to deter others. Thus Hermes.
In God you should trust both the beginning and the end of your matters. Thus Gregory.
Whenever you would begin to do something well, you should begin by asking God what would be good for you. Thus Pythagoras.
The face shows what lies in the heart more than the word. Thus Homer.
The opinions and sayings of diverse philosophers

Do not expose yourself to sleeping until you have considered the work that you have done that day, so you may know if you have erred, and in what, and if you have done something you ought not to have done. And if you found that you have done wrong, you should lament it, and if it was good, you should rejoice, and through this you will know how you stand with God. Thus Aristotle.

A just king reigns well. A king who does the right thing and serves justice, rules the will of the people, but if he does injustice and violence, his kingdom will search for another to rule in his stead. It is fitting for a lord to rectify himself first, rather than his people. Thus Zelon.

It is fitting to act properly: to think at night of good policy, and to execute the plan by day. And he who has servants or subjects and governs them well, him you should establish as leader of your army; and he who possesses hereditary lands and manages them well, him you should establish as manager of your revenue. Thus Plato.

The just fear no one. For that reason, he who follows justice does not have to fear anything. Therefore some people have said that the just have no reason to fear God, and no reason to imitate and obey his command. And if the king is not just, he is not a king, but a thief and violent plunderer. Thus Aristotle.

To govern a people is not fit for a boy, nor for him who is ignorant of worldly affairs, nor for him who often changes his desires, nor for him who desires to conquer many people. There is no difference between the age of boys and the manners of boys, because the manners of men do not depend on time, but on whether he follows his desires in his acts. He who does not follow his own desires where, when, how much, and how something should be, is good at governing. Thus Aristotle.
You should always remember that your soul should be in noble thought; some thoughts are after all hostile to your sublime state. Thus Pythagoras.

Beware of those who do not live according to truth: even though they hear truth, they do not act on it. And you should not prepare traps in order to harm men, nor make attempts to cause them damage. Because this is a matter that will not be concealed; and although it is not known from the start, it will be known in the end. Thus Hermes.
Unfortunate and unhappy in this world is he who lacks a sense of wisdom and doctrine. Thus Hermes.

It is fitting that you honor every person according to his condition, his distinction, and according to his intelligence, by revealing the honor that you did to him, so that praiseworthy deeds are also revealed to the people. Thus Hermes.
Honor is made by the honorable. Aristotle.
Do not unreasonably impose punishment on a sinner, but leave some space for him to exculpate himself. Thus Hermes.

When a king cannot repress his own desires, how can he restrain the desires of others? And he who cannot restrain his own failures, cannot restrain people who are distant from him. Therefore it behooves a king to start by ruling himself and thereafter to extend his rule over others. Thus Hermes.

If you do not rectify yourself first, you cannot rectify your people, nor will you be able to govern them while you are wandering. Indeed, how would the blind be able to lead another, the poor to enrich another; how would the dishonored, or the one lacking honor, honor someone, and how can the weak strengthen the weak with his powers? Certainly, no one will ever be able to direct others unless he knows and directs himself first. So if you want to dispel the sins of others, first expel them from your heart. Because while the sin is still in your soul, you cannot purge another, if you do not want to act like a doctor who is afflicted by a disease, and struggles to care for another, while he cannot cure himself of the same. Thus Aristotle.

In doing as you should not do, dislike arises from your rule; out of dislike comes forth falsehood, out of falsehood hate; truly, hate begets injustice, out of injustice comes forth enmity, out of enmity war; through war, law perishes and livelihoods are lost. And by doing precisely what should be done, truth is produced by rule; justice proceeds from truth, and from justice love comes forth; from love, truly, gifts proceed and protection arises: with these things, the law is upheld, and the world is made greater for the people. Aristotle.
How are friends obtained? By honoring them when they are present, and by doing good to them, and by praising them when they are absent. Thus Zelon.
He who is of good morals, has a good and secure life, and men respect him; and he who is of bad morals has a bad life, and men flee him. Thus Socrates.

He who rules over men always needs to remember three things: the first is the number of people that are under his rule; the second is that, though they are under his rule, they are free, and not servants; the third is that his rule cannot last except for a short time. Thus Hermes.

You should know that the people obey him who is good to them, and that it cannot go well with the kingdom unless you do good to the people. Because when the lord lacks this, he will only be lord of himself. Thus Hermes.
At any time of indignation, a foul word should never come out of your mouth, because that is dishonest and leads to punishment. Thus Hermes.

Better and more noble is a good reputation in this world, and exclusion from punishment in the other world. It is stronger to remain silent than to speak while being ignorant, and to seek solitude rather than to attach oneself to bad things. Wisdom is thus acquired, and humility, and good favor, and piety, and liberation of sins. Thus Hermes.
What is felt is shown by the speech. Thus Loginon.
And from the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks. Thus Homer.
And the mouth shows what lies in the heart. Thus Socrates.
For three things kings are honored: for the institution of good laws, for conquering good regions, and for populating deserted regions. Thus Aristotle.

You should not examine the deeds of men very strictly, because, since people cannot be entirely free of faults if they are completely and severely examined, your judgment will be confused. Therefore your eyes should be turned away from some of their faults, in order to forgive them. After all, while they are under your rule, their hearts will be guided and they will proceed for the better by your doing. Thus Aristotle.

The ignorance of a man is revealed in three ways: by not having a thought for rectifying himself, and by not opposing his desires, and by governing himself by the counsel of his wife, both in the things which he knows and in the things which he does not know. Thus Socrates.

It is fitting for a king to know those who are close to him, each of whom he appoints to a position according to his discretion, wisdom, and happiness, providing for everyone who is deserving according to their need, and these gifts should not be unacceptable or displeasing. Thus Hermes.
Cheerfulness is the sign of understanding and the opposite. Thus Hermes.
It is not fitting for a man to hate, nor to offend someone who offends him: on the contrary, his behavior and words should do well and pacify. Thus Hermes.

When a friend makes a mistake in your presence, you should not withdraw yourself from his friendship, as long as something remains in him through which you can see that he will be able to rectify himself. Thus Aristotle.
Committing himself to his acquittal and effort (i.e., doing his best to make up for his mistakes)

A wise king rules with gentleness and forgiveness, for he does not rule with displeasure, haughtiness, and with things that are only good for himself; and this is because he resolves to do right and equal justice. Thus Hermes.
If a king has accumulated wealth and will not spend it where he should, he will either lose that wealth or the kingdom. Thus Hermes.

Two things are praiseworthy and good: law and wisdom, because by law we are held back from sins, and through wisdom we acquire all good virtues. A good king is he who does not permit one to offend another. Thus Aristotle.
You should not laugh a lot, nor become angry, because those are the two works of foolishness. Aristotle.

It is fitting for a king to receive into his service those whom, before he reigned, he knew as good and trustworthy. Because a king, after he has started to reign, cannot recognize these people well, since then they all flatter and honor him. Thus Socrates.
He who deems all men the same cannot have friends. Thus Socrates.
He who governs himself well is fit to be a governor. Thus Plato.
A man suffers for three reasons: for a rich man to come to poverty; for an honorable man to incur contempt; for a wise man to be mocked by the ignorant. Thus Plato.
Do not wait to do good to those who deserve it until you are required to, but do good to them from yourself. Thus Plato.

Do not suddenly become angry, because if you are accustomed to do so, anger will rule you. If you are able, you should avoid anger, because it does not let you see the outcome of something. Thus Plato.
If you want to know someone’s nature, you should consult with him about something; and from that you will know his iniquity or equity, and his goodness or wickedness. Thus Plato.
You should know that among God’s gifts, wisdom is the more excellent: love wisdom, and listen to the wise, and obey God. Thus Plato.

You should attempt to bring your adversary, who is plotting against you, to justice, rather than to seek vengeance. For vengeance is harmful to both, and preserving justice is beneficial to both. Thus Plato.
Bring men to justice pleasantly; otherwise you will be at struggle and war with them. Thus Plato.
He who is not tamed by or does not resign himself to pleasant reproof, tame him with ugly and harsh reproof. Thus Hermes.

Do not be served by someone in any way that is not natural to him, even though he is obliged by debt. This is because many will become restless with you when their work requires them to do something for which they are not suited. Thus Plato.

You should not support him who, while being protected by you, intends something that will diminsh your goodness or makes you less appreciated. Indeed, in all other cases you should advance and help him. Thus Plato.

You should never think that your enemy has only little power, because greater harm can come from him than you would think. An unnatural thing has greater powers at the start, and a natural thing is stronger at the end. Thus Plato.

div.note: Dominion of the wicked is not good, for although it may seem good at certain times, it nevertheless comes to a bad end. Thus Plato.

note.gloss: The greater harm that can befall a kingdom is through those who, with a proud heart, hold a better position than they deserve, for they despise others who are better than them, and thus the order of the king is subverted and upset. Thus Plato.

Safe is he who serves kings in faithfulness and serves the people with piety. And he will not lose the position he is in, neither for any good fortune that he has, nor because of some misfortune that he despairs of or that weighs him down. Thus Plato.
You should consult with him who is equal to you in his affairs, because he best understands what you need. Thus Plato.

A moderate shame makes a man give up that which is not appropriate for him; too much of it makes him give up that which is appropriate for him; but too little shame causes him to adopt that which is not appropriate for him. Thus Plato.
You should not use deeds when words suffice. Thus Plato.

Drunkenness is deemed forbidden for a king. Since a king should be the guardian of the kingdom, how disgraceful would it be if he does not have self-control! Among kings, happy is he who governs the kingdom of his predecessors, and unhappy he who lost it and is deprived of it. Thus Plato.
You should not allow yourself to do anything until your sense has foreseen it can be done pleasantly. Thus Plato.
It behooves a judge not to be rigid in his speech against the perpetrators of a crime, because if he does not behave as such, he would abuse his authority. Thus Plato.
Like the king, so his people. The wishes and desires of men can be found in the wishes and desires of kings themselves. Thus Plato.
How is the just man known? By this: that he does not do something harmful to another, nor speaks a falsehood for his own profit. Thus Plato.
If a king neglects to investigate the deeds of his people, his army, and his enemies, not one day will he be secure in his reign. Thus Hermes.
How good is that people, whose king is of good judgment, and good counsel, and wise in knowledge; and how wretched is the same when he lacks any of the aforementioned. Thus Hermes.

When a king disregards a little thing which he ought to do, it will grow worse. Just as a mild illness of the body which is not treated with medicine will grow and disturb the whole body. Thus Hermes.

It is important to instruct the son of a king in knowledge, so that he may preserve his kingdom, and so that he may be just to his people, and so that he may direct his army. And he should not be allowed to enjoy hunting too much, nor other wanderings, and he should be instructed to speak calmly and to avoid using falsehoods. Thus Hermes.

It is important for a king that his favors are shown to good men, and to those who strive to obtain knowledge, so that they, for this reason, will continue to change for the benefit of the king. Thus Hermes.

It is important for a king, when he wants to be served by someone in his employment, to first know his morals and how he conducts himself, his house, and his family. And if he finds him to be of good morals, and a governor of his estates and observer of laws, and if he patiently bears the misfortunes that befall him, the king should make sure that he is served by him. If not, turn him away. Thus Hermes.
Cherish the pure soul who cherishes you, because he is better than a brother from your father and mother who wishes for your death so that he may inherit your possessions. Thus Hermes.
He who is lacking in what is due to his creator, how much more does he lack in all other good deeds? Thus Hermes.
In sleeping much there is no profit, only damage. Accustom yourself therefore to do good both day and night, so that you do not spend half your life in idleness.
Blessed is that king who changes his laws for the better, and better and more noble is the king who, during his reign, changes a bad law into a good one. Thus Hermes.
Say well of your friend whom you wish to meet, for the beginning of love is to speak well and the beginning of hate is to speak badly. Thus Socrates.
The greater rectification is to guide a king to distance himself from evil things, lest the bad things that happen are attributed to him. Thus Socrates.
The king is like a great river, springing forth from a small one, so that if he is sweet, all small ones will be sweet, and if salty, all will be salty. Thus Plato.
You should not pass a judgment before you heard both claimants. Thus Plato.
When you have a friend, it is good that you are a friend to him, but it is not good if you are an enemy to your enemy. Thus Plato.

If you are pious, then do not do so with such piety that it could be turned into damage. And you should not delay to inflict punishment on those who deserve it; and work at strengthening the law, because therein stands the fear of the lord. Aristotle.

You should consider the weaker of your enemies stronger than yourself. Similarly, you should look after your army, as someone who needs it for their protection because of great arising causes. Thus Aristotle.
If you want to become a wise king, you should not turn to the rude and ignorant, but to those who surpass you in wisdom. Thus Asseron.
The world is not eternal: therefore, when you are able to do good, you should not delay it, and you should focus on having a good reputation. Thus Hippocrates.

You should not be a spender like the ignorant one who has some possessions; nor should you be frugal, so that you do not become a slave. But in all things you should have moderation, because in all things a measure is useful. Thus Pythagoras.
You should not be suspicious, because suspicion between you and any one of your friends tears away love. Thus Loginon.
A friend will be known in times of need, because in a time of joy anyone is a friend. Thus Diogenes.

A kingdom is lost for four reasons: if the roots are neglected by the king, and he is only focused on the management of the branches, the kingdom is lost; and when he puts his trust in fortune, thus neglecting the actions that are necessary, the kingdom is lost; and when he is not at all directed to the population of the earth, the kingdom is lost; and because of long duration of wars, the kingdom is lost. Thus Plato.
Your favors given to good men lead to repayment, and the gifts given to vile men lead them to desire for more. Thus Plato.

It is not fitting for a king to put his trust in someone who despises him, nor in someone who is very greedy, nor in someone who deserves punishment for something and has made a mistake, nor in someone who has deprived him of his dominion and of good things, nor in someone who has suffered damages because of his behavior, nor in someone who has made an alliance with his enemy. Indeed, it is important not to concede power to such men, and if it is possible, to avoid their judgment on anything that concerns them. Thus Asseron.

It is fitting for a king to be studious and careful in looking after his kingdom and his people like a gardener looks after his garden. And it is fitting for a king that he is the first to show the laws that apply to his people by giving a good example to them. Thus Pythagoras.

It is fitting for a king not to value himself too much, nor to be governed by his council, nor to enjoy the hunt frequently, nor to take a path which he does not know, or a narrow one, on a dark night. And he should be cheerful of expression, willingly beholding men, and he should greet them, and converse pleasantly, because the people pay much attention to that. Thus Pythagoras.
Do everything with counsel. Thus Solomon.

You should beware of eating and drinking, and of the power of very jealous people and other wicked ones, but not of him who is secure in trust and feeling, and of those who love him and his lordship. Thus Pythagoras.
If you want to correct someone, you should not act like a man who desires to have vengeance on another, but rather you should act like someone who wishes to correct himself. Thus Diogenes.

You should know for sure that the fear of God is the greater wisdom and greater delight. And it is that from which flows all good, and which opens the gates of comprehension and perception of the law, and you cannot be just if you do not have the fear of God. You should employ wisdom and follow the law, accustom yourself with clemency and equip yourself with good lessons, and consider well in all your matters, and your mind will be protected from the servitude of ignorance and the servitude of youth. Thus Hermes.
Make your sons learn from an early age, before they grow much older and are dragged down by wickedness, and you will not fail in this. Thus Hermes.

And when you all celebrate a feast, being happy with your family in your household, you should remember the poor by bestowing gifts and favors, and comfort the needy and the unfortunate. You should ransom captives, cure the sick, clothe the naked, feed the hungry, let the thirsty drink, receive pilgrims, satisfy creditors, compensate those who suffer injustice, and not bring affliction to the afflicted; indeed, you should comfort and please them with agreeable and honorable deeds. Thus Hermes.
Guard yourself against the company of the wicked, and the jealous, and the drunk, and the ignorant. Thus Hermes.
You should not associate yourself with the wicked, because your nature will, without your notice, take something from his nature. Thus Plato.

Do not make liars swear, because you will be sharing in their sins when you know that he denies the truth. Likewise, it is not fitting for a king to employ a deceitful man, or a wicked one. Thus Hermes.

If you see any harm or any fault in someone, you should not disgrace him or mock him, but return to God, because you are all created from the same matter, and he who mocks cannot be sure that, in time, he does not make the same mistake. Therefore it is fitting, when you have seen it, to raise your eyes to God, thanking him for the salvation given to you, and asking for mercy, so that he may protect you. And beware of mockery, because from that proceeds hate. Thus Hermes.
Threefold are the works of the wise: to make a friend out of an enemy, knowledge out of ignorance, and good out of bad. Thus Hermes.

No one who is not pious is fit to rule. It is fitting for a king not to give power or lordship to those who do not have piety; and because of that he will love all, like a good father does his good sons. Thus Hermes.
The life of a man is so short that he should not hate anyone. Thus Hermes.
And you should treat your friends with love, truly, and not at any moment show a sign of hate. Socrates.
If someone would not do well to his friends when he can, they will leave him when he needs them. Thus Plato.
There are three things that harm a king: overmuch drinking of wine, frequent listening to music, and excessive love for his wife. Thus Hermes.
A king who makes his rule subject to law is fit to reign, and he who makes the law subject to his rule, he harms his own rule. Thus Aristotle.

Whenever you want to ask someone for counsel on your deeds, first investigate him, and how he governs himself in his deeds; because if you see that he does not control his mind, and does not dedicate himself to obtain some goodness, he will be even more neglectful with your matters, when he deems you of lesser worth than himself. Thus Socrates.
Be vigilant in your counsel, because to sleep in this is to share in death. Thus Pythagoras.

You should beware not to rely only on your own counsel; but you should consult him who is of good discretion and advancing age, and experienced in many things. And you should use counsel of different people. And if you have found out what is right from one of them, accept this. Generally, you should guide yourself according to the more useful things you heard through counsel after all considerations, and God will guide you. Thus Hermes.
Why does the sensible man seek counsel? Because he fears his own desire, and fears that his feeling is mixed up with his reason. Thus Socrates.
You should not give someone power over yourself, because if you have given power to a friend so that he may place his feet above your feet, tomorrow he will place them above your neck. Thus Diogenes.

It is fitting for a king to withdraw from his people, and not to keep company with them as if they are friends. Otherwise he will be despised, for the nature of the people is to despise each other and those who keep company with them, so that they will judge anyone who keeps company with them the same as themselves. Too much familiarity breeds contempt. Thus Plato.
You should not associate yourself with anything but with what is right, so that your deeds are true and not mockery. Thus Hermes.
And receive those who seek the truth as friends. Thus Pythagoras.

Through wisdom is acquired humility, good will, piety, and privation of sins. He who does not seek wisdom through reading, but thinks to acquire it through many other things, is wrong and ignorant. Thus Hermes.
Good counsel shows, at the beginning, the end of a thing. Thus Socrates.

He who keeps a secret, is discreet, and he who discloses it, is foolish. It is fitting for a man to keep a secret that is revealed to him. And more pleasing is he who keeps a secret, even if he is not obliged by it. And keeping a secret is the nobility of the mind. When your heart does not keep your own secret, it will be held even less in the hearts of others. Thus Socrates.
A man learns more every day by experiencing what happens to him. It is enough for a man to know what he sees of the world, and from this, on any day he can obtain new knowledge. Thus Socrates.
He who esteems God with honest love and loves wisdom itself and good deeds, God honors him; and he does good to him who is thoughtful. Thus Aristotle.
You should wish to rectify another, if you can, as you would desire to rectify yourself, because this is the honor and nobility of your mind. Aristotle.
It is fitting for a lord to rectify himself first and then his people. Thus Zelon.
If you want your love to be durable with anyone, you should instruct him to do well. Thus Enesius.

A man can control himself when he knows himself, because it is the highest wisdom for a man to have self-knowledge, so that he is not deceived by self-love or considers himself good when he is not. After all, we see that many think themselves strong and honorable while they are not, and they generally all consider themselves more discreet than others. And he who thus thinks of himself is of small discretion. Thus Galen.
Bringing good governance to everything else
Who is just and who sensible? Just is he who can do injustice, but does not; and sensible or discreet is he who knows, from among all things, that which is right for human nature. Thus Galen.

Lest a man is enraged, he should be continually reminded that he cannot always be obeyed, but that he must sometimes obey someone else, and that he cannot always be served, but that he must serve someone else, nor can he always be paid by someone. And because God examines everyone, you should consider these things, and not be troubled by anger, and be only a little disturbed, if you are upset. Thus Tesilius.
You should strive to reconcile yourself with your enemies, even though you are sure of your strength and power. Thus Maedarges.

If a king acts justly and rightfully, he will rule the souls of his people. And if he commits injustice and unfairness, he will show himself outwardly as a king, but in their hearts they turn away to another ruler. Thus Enesius.

When someone considers you good, strive to prove him true; and you should consider him to be good who has chosen to esteem you, whether he is humble or elevated. He who does not rule his own mind when he is in company cannot rule many others. Thus Enesius.

div.note: In this world, there is nothing worse than to lack generosity and doctrine. Thus Maedarges.

note.gloss: It is fitting for anyone to continually scrutinize his own deeds, and to strive to know what those near him think of him, and especially those who sell and those who keep company with him, and in what ways they scold or praise him. Because when he does this, none of his crimes will escape his notice. Thus Aristotle.

In ten ways, God is served, and they are these: give thanks if anything is given to you; if you suffer misfortune, endure it patiently; if you speak, speak the truth; do what you have promised; if you pass judgment, judge rightly; keep measure; if you can, you should do good before it is needed; honor your friends; indulge your friends and the faults of your enemies; and do not do unto your friend what you do not want for yourself. Thus Aristotle.
When your discretion holds you back from doing something, you should not ignore it. This is because it will be a greater sin when it is discovered that you did what it had forbidden. Thus Plato.
By three things, a wise man is known: because of the things that he knows, because he does not hold himself of great value, nor is enraged by any mockery, nor elevated when he is praised. Thus Plato.
When a king conquers his enemies, it is fitting that he follows good customs, namely in justice, in generosity of wealth, in patience, in diligence, and in other good customs. Thus Hermes.

When you serve any lord, do not become equal to him except in faith, in feeling, in patience; in all other things, truly, by no means. You should beware, lest he observes you (to try to be) equal to himself in rank or clothing, or in his delights. Thus Plato.
If you seek to treat your enemy with contempt, you should not damage yourself instead of your enemy. Thus Pythagoras.

A good man gives thanks for good gifts according to the capacity of the giver and the satisfaction of the recipient. A vile man, truly, does not give thanks except according to the quality of the benefactor. Thus Plato.

Some kings keep always the rank of one kind among their subjects in favor, and in this they are very much deceived, and they err, because one kind of man is not fixed in the same condition and rank. Indeed, their goodness grows less, similar to the seed of one kind that is scattered on the earth and corrupted and changed through the march of time. Thus Plato.
It is good to speak little, complete with reason, and to respond laudably and immediately. Thus Aristotle.
The fornicator cannot be praised, nor can the cheerful be angry, nor the honorable envious, nor can the greedy be wealthy. Thus Aristotle.
Wisdom adorns the wealth of the wealthy, and conceals the poverty of the poor. Thus Aristotle.
There is nothing less fitting for a king than to plunder, because a king should conduct himself like a father. Thus Aristotle.
The wicked obey out of fear, the good out of kindness. So, knowing these two ways, you should willingly show kindness to the one, and to the other, truly, punishment. Thus Aristotle.

You should rule your people by doing good, because your rule will be more durable; provide for them rather than oppress them. Because while you previously ruled their bodies, you will rule their hearts through the favors that you grant them. And you should know that presumptuous people easily fall from word to deed; therefore, make sure that they do not fall to the word, so it follows that they do not fall to the deed. Thus Aristotle.

You should promote observers of the faith as well as the true laws, and because of this, you will be considered competent in this world, and in all things you will obtain the desired end. And refrain from bad things, because then you will rule both laws and the people. Thus Aristotle.
How disgraceful is it to announce something and not do it, and how honorable to perform the deeds before the words. Thus Ptolemy.

Philosophers asked emperor Alexander how he was able to control, at such a tender age, such a large kingdom. He answered: because, being reunited with my enemies, I have made friends, and I have satisfied my friends with favors. Thus Ptolemy.

If the king’s counselor and his (the king’s) physician would follow his desires entirely, he (the king) will always be injured and continually infirm, cheated by the expectation of a good end. Thus Asseron.

It is fitting for a king to commit his affairs to him of whose faith and opinion he has approved, and if he cannot have such a one, he should commit them (his affairs) to him who keeps company with good wise men. Thus Asseron.

For him who lives splendidly with the king, and dwells in magnificence, it is impossible that weakness does not affect him. Therefore a wise king should take care that, when he hears that someone has committed an offense against him, not one hour passes before he is certain of the truth or falsehood of this person, and similarly, of the magnitude of the offense, and whether it was done consciously or out of error, and if it is of such nature that it becomes something which should not be indulged. Thus Asseron.

It is good for servants to show their king their virtue and faith and nobility of birth, so that the king, aware of the status and condition of each of them, can entrust his tasks to them and, when it is needed, order them to perform them. And if the king does not reward the obedient and the faithful and the non-deserving according to their merits, but instead he advances some for retribution, while others are frightened because of the severity of their punishment, he ought not to be regarded as king nor as someone who does what needs to be done. Thus Asseron.
He who does not keep the king from wrongdoing, and conceals the truth from his doctor, and does not tell his friend a secret that he ought to tell, he destroys himself. Thus Asseron.
Though it is sometimes sorely troubled

If a king is fortunate, his affairs will be done well, and if wise, wisdom will be made stronger in time, and if true, the people will have cause to rejoice, and if just, his reign lasts. Thus Asseron.
It is very difficult to obtain a kingdom, but it is more difficult to know how to conserve it. Thus Asseron.

It is good for a wise man who is with the king that if he sees him do anything harmful to himself or the kingdom or his people, to recite histories and exemplars that touch on a similar matter, so that he refrains from such an action, and so that he presently replies that he sees that it is said for him. Thus Asseron.
Honor the good; from this, after all, you will obtain the love of the people. Thus Aristotle.

Of good discretion, and strong mind, and laudable faith is he who faced adversities when they arrived, because what a man is like is not shown in prosperity. Therefore, take courage from that which supports you and from the fact that God absolves you from diseases, and do not refuse the gifts which he has brought to you. Thus Aristotle.

Generosity is to give to the needy and deserving, according to the possibility of the giver. Because he who gives beyond possibility is not generous, but truly a waster; and he who gives to those who do not need it is not acceptable, but he is like someone who pours water into the sea. Thus Aristotle.

div.note: The beginnings of goodness are bitter, until the end, when they are truly sweet. The beginnings of depravity are sweet, until the end, when they are truly bitter. Thus Plato.

note.gloss: From habit, some men think each thing bad, and some good; except fidelity, which everyone thinks good. Thus Plato.

The goodness of good men in turn encourages good men to love, while the malice of malicious men in turn encourages others to hate. Thus you can see that the truthful loves the truthful, and the faithful the faithful. The liar, truly, abhors the liar, and the thief captures the thief, because he does not want to keep company with him on account of his iniquity. Thus Plato.

You should be lawful to him who commits himself to you, and faithful to him who trusts you, and then you will be sure to avoid a bad end. And because of this truthfulness and lawfulness, your friends will honor you, and by leaving that which is not profitable, your goodness will be complete. Thus Socrates.
You cannot take back what you have said, nor what you have done. Therefore, you should be careful for yourself. Thus Socrates.

Sorrow comes from three things: of which the first is a good man who is ruled by a bad man, and this is always sorrowful for him who sees or hears it; and the other is a wise man governed by the depraved, who is always in labor and sadness; and the third is the generous man who needs to ask the greedy, because he is in great anguish. Thus Socrates.
The affairs of men go wrong when good counsel is with him who is not heard, and arms with him who does not use them, and wealth with him who does not spend it. Thus Socrates.

You should follow good works, and learn wisdom from the better men who are present in your time, avoiding the snare which women prepare for men, which is a hindrance to and destroyer of wisdom and results in a bad state. Thus Socrates.
You should not bestow your gifts except to the right people, because many simple men support those who do not need it while they ought to support those who do need it. Thus Socrates.
Knowledge is better than ignorance, because through knowledge a person avoids falling into the fire, and through ignorance he proceeds to sink down into the abyss. Thus Homer.

div.note: This world is the home of trade, and it is unfortunate for him who departs from it with ruin. Thus Homer.

note.gloss: Gentleness of speech dispels boredom. Thus Homer.

He who does not exalt himself for his nobility, appearance, riches, or lordship, and makes the intention of his words equal to his deeds, him God will elevate, as well as his successors who follow after him. Thus Hermes.
The mistake of a wise man is like the breaking of a ship which, when it is sunk, causes many to drown. Thus Hermes.

Just as it is fitting for the king’s dignity that the people committed to him are obedient to him, so it is fitting that the king is concerned with their situation before his own, because he is as near to them as the soul is to the body. Thus Hermes.

He who relies on the world because of his own disposition should not be required to give counsel, for he will only give the judgment of his own will. Because the love of him who does not change the world is intellectual; and the love of him who does change the world is wilfull. Thus Socrates.
If you do not want your son or servant to err, you desire something that is beyond nature. Thus Pythagoras.

A man is safer from silence than from speaking a lot because through speech he can fall into errors. This does not apply to the wise man when he speaks, but an ignorant man errs when he wants to speak either a lot or a little. And the advantage of being silent is greater than the advantage of speaking, and the damage of speaking is greater than the damage of being silent. And the wise man is known from much taciturnity, and the ignorant man from much speaking. And he who is not silent from himself will be forced to be silent by another and will be less appreciated; and he who is silent until he is asked to speak is better than he who speaks until he is ordered to be silent. Words are under a man’s control until he speaks, after which they escape from his control. And if a man speaks, it is known whether he is perfect or flawed; and if he is silent, it is doubtful what he is like. And he who wants to speak should first consider; he should inspect his words, because it is better that he inspects them himself than another. And your speech will be heard, so you should strive to speak rightly, or you should remain silent. And he who is silent scrutinizes the speech of another. And he who suffers knows from his speech that he is hurt. Thus Socrates.
Employ good manners, and you will be loved. And even though you may be ugly, the beauty of your manners will surpass the appearance of your figure. Thus Socrates.

He who fills his mind with love of the world fills it with three things: that is to say, with poverty, which he will never avoid if he seeks riches; and trust, which he will never attain in the end; and impediment without success. Thus Socrates.
He is not patient who is burdened in such a way that he can endure it and has endured it; but he who is burdened beyond the capacity of his nature and has endured it is patient. Thus Pythagoras.
You should not continue your efforts to obtain great delights, because you will not be able to endure adversities when they come. Thus Pythagoras.
Rejoice in your ears, and for this reason: you have received two ears and one mouth, so that you would hear more than speak. Thus Diogenes.
Do not put your trust in the world, because it never fulfilled what it had promised to your predecessors, and it will do the same to you. Thus Socrates.
